Crowds that gathered outside the morgue's viewing window were, by most contemporary accounts, only rarely there because they recognized someone; far more often, they were there simply to look, drawn by the same impulse that would later fill wax museum chambers of horrors and, in a very different register, motivates the continued fascination with death masks that this book is itself an exploration of. The identification of the unclaimed dead and the entertainment of the curious living occupied, uncomfortably, the very same physical space.

section.subtitle: A Face Without a Name, Revisited
section.paragraph: It was from within this exact institutional and cultural context — a public morgue accustomed to displaying unidentified bodies for a mixture of practical and voyeuristic reasons — that the story of *L'Inconnue de la Seine*, the Unknown Woman of the Seine, first introduced in Chapter 1, took shape. According to the long-circulating account, a young woman's body, recovered from the river and never identified, was displayed at the Paris morgue sometime in the late nineteenth century, and a mask-maker, struck by the unusually serene and faintly smiling expression on her face, took a plaster cast that was subsequently reproduced and sold, eventually finding its way into artists' studios and private homes across Europe.

As already noted, very little of this narrative can be independently verified through documented historical sources. No confirmed record establishes her actual identity, the precise circumstances or even cause of her death, or the specific date and location of the casting itself, and some researchers have seriously questioned whether the mask was taken from a corpse at all, suggesting instead that it may have been modeled from a living subject and only later attached, through popular retelling, to the romantic legend of an anonymous drowning victim. What can be documented with much greater confidence is the mask's extraordinary cultural afterlife from the early twentieth century onward: reproductions of her face became fashionable decorative objects in bohemian artistic circles, and her image — an unidentified young woman, apparently at peace despite the implied violence of her presumed death — inspired a substantial body of poetry, prose, and visual art across the twentieth century, precisely because her lack of a confirmed identity left so much open to imaginative interpretation. In one of the more genuinely strange turns in this book's entire history, her face was later adopted, in the middle of the twentieth century, as the model for a training mannequin used in cardiopulmonary resuscitation instruction, meaning that whoever she actually was, her preserved features have quite plausibly been seen, and even physically practiced upon, by an extraordinary number of people across the world.

keypoints.title: Key Point: Separating the Documented from the Legendary
keypoints.point: Documented: a mask matching this description circulated widely in Europe from the late nineteenth century onward and inspired significant literary and artistic responses across the twentieth century.
Undocumented or disputed: her specific identity, the exact circumstances and cause of her death, the precise date of casting, and even whether the mask was taken from a deceased person at all.
The gap between these two categories is itself part of the story — her fame rests as much on the space left open by uncertainty as on any verified biographical fact.

section.subtitle: Whose Face Is This, and Who Decides?
section.paragraph: The stories gathered in this chapter raise a question that this book has touched on before but that deserves to be stated directly here: who has the right to decide what happens to a dead person's face, particularly when that person cannot advocate for themselves and left behind no family in a position to do so? For the executed criminals studied by nineteenth-century phrenologists, the answer, in practice, was the state and the scientific establishment, operating within a legal and social framework that afforded the condemned essentially no protection over how their remains might be used after punishment had been carried out. For the unidentified dead displayed at the Paris morgue, the answer was, in effect, no one in particular — a gap in accountability filled instead by institutional practicality and public curiosity, with the person's own interests, whatever they might have been, entirely unrepresented in the process.

This is not a comfortable observation, and this book does not intend to make it one. It is included specifically because any honest history of the death mask has to reckon with the fact that the same basic technique — capturing a face in plaster after death — served radically different ethical purposes depending on who the subject was, how much social power they or their families held, and how willing the society around them was to treat their remains with the same consideration extended, almost automatically, to the famous and the wealthy. Modern museum and archival practice, examined in much greater depth in a later chapter of this book, has increasingly had to confront exactly this imbalance, asking what obligations institutions now holding these objects owe to the memory of people who never had any say in how their faces would be used.

section.subtitle: What Comes Next
section.paragraph: The scientific interest that surfaced repeatedly throughout this chapter — in the skulls and faces of condemned criminals, in the theories of phrenology and physiognomy that shaped how those objects were studied — represents only the earlier, cruder stage of a much longer, more consequential story. The next chapter turns directly to that story: the gradual development, over the second half of the nineteenth century and into the twentieth, of genuinely reliable methods of identifying the dead, from measurement systems that built directly on the flawed assumptions already introduced in this book, to the far more rigorous forensic techniques — fingerprinting prominent among them — that would eventually replace the death mask itself as a tool of identification, even as the mask's older, more emotional purposes endured alongside them.

chapter.title: Death Masks and the Birth of Forensic Identification
chapter.epigraph: For most of the nineteenth century, identifying an unknown body meant trusting a stranger's memory, a family's grief, or the accuracy of someone's eye. By the century's end, an entirely new science had set out to replace all three with numbers.

section.subtitle: A Science in Search of Certainty
section.paragraph: Picture a small, cluttered office within the Paris Prefecture of Police, sometime in the 1880s — a reconstructed scene, representative of a practice that became increasingly formalized during this decade, rather than a record of any single documented visit. A clerk positions a seated man against a measuring apparatus, calling out figures as an assistant records them in a ledger: the length and breadth of the skull, the span of the outstretched arms, the length of the left foot, the length of the left middle finger, the length of the left forearm. The man being measured is not a corpse. He is a living suspect, recently arrested, and the ritual being performed on him belongs to an ambitious new system that its inventor believed could finally solve one of the most persistent practical problems facing nineteenth-century police work: how to reliably prove that the person standing in front of you today is the same person who was arrested, under a different name, several years before.

This chapter turns to that problem directly, and to the systems — some scientifically sound, others deeply flawed — that nineteenth- and early twentieth-century Europe developed to solve it. The death mask and the broader tradition of facial casting examined throughout this book sit at the edge of this story rather than its center, but the connection between them is real and worth tracing carefully, because the same cultural moment that produced the elaborate collecting culture of death masks also produced the first serious attempts at what we would now call forensic identification, and the two pursuits were, for several decades, far more entangled than most popular accounts acknowledge.

section.subtitle: Alphonse Bertillon and the Grammar of the Body
section.paragraph: The system being performed in the scene above belonged to Alphonse Bertillon, a French police record clerk who, in the early 1880s, developed what became known as anthropometry, or more informally, Bertillonage: a method of identifying individuals through a standardized set of precise bodily measurements, combined with detailed, systematized descriptions of physical features, including the shape of the ear, the color of the eyes, and other distinguishing marks. Bertillon's underlying insight was reasonably sound in principle — that the combination of several independent physical measurements, each varying naturally across a population, would produce a set of figures unique enough, in combination, to distinguish one individual from millions of others, in an era before any comparably reliable biometric alternative existed.

Bertillon's system was adopted with real enthusiasm by police forces across France and, before long, in other countries as well, and it represented a genuine methodological advance over what had preceded it: essentially, the memory and personal judgment of individual police officers and witnesses, supplemented at best by written physical descriptions that varied enormously in detail and reliability from one record to the next. For roughly two decades, anthropometric measurement stood as the most rigorous identification technology available to European and American law enforcement, and it is worth recognizing this achievement honestly, even though, as this chapter will discuss, the system's dominance would prove considerably shorter-lived than its inventor hoped.

Bertillon is also significant to this book's story for a second, related reason: he was instrumental in standardizing what became known as forensic or judicial photography — the practice of taking consistent, front-facing and profile photographs of arrested suspects, taken under controlled lighting and framing conditions specifically designed to allow reliable comparison across different arrests and different years. This standardized photograph, still recognizable today as the modern mug shot, represented a direct and largely successful competitor to an older, cruder tradition already discussed in the previous chapter: the practice of displaying or casting the faces of the unidentified and the criminal for purposes of recognition. Where a nineteenth-century police morgue had relied on the public simply walking past a body and hoping for recognition, and where earlier collections of criminal masks had relied on the (largely discredited) hope that a skull's shape might reveal criminal character, Bertillon's photographic system offered something genuinely new: a fast, cheap, reproducible, and comparatively objective visual record, one that did not require an artist's hours of careful plaster work, and that could be filed, copied, and distributed to other police departments with far greater ease than any physical cast.

keypoints.title: Key Point: Photography Did What the Death Mask Could Not
keypoints.point: A death mask required time, skill, and materials, and produced a single, heavy, easily damaged physical object.
A standardized police photograph could be produced in minutes, copied cheaply, and mailed or telegraphed to other jurisdictions — a practical advantage that mattered enormously to police work.

This practical gap is a major reason why, by the early twentieth century, the death mask had largely lost its earlier role as a tool of criminal or forensic identification, even as its symbolic and memorial functions endured.

section.subtitle: The Face Enters the Police File
section.paragraph: The rise of forensic photography under Bertillon and his contemporaries marks a genuinely important turning point in this book's larger story, because it represents the moment when the practical work of identifying bodies — living suspects and unidentified dead alike — began to separate decisively from the older tradition of the physical facial cast. For most of the century examined in the previous chapter, a death mask taken from an unidentified body, or the public display of the body itself, had represented one of the only realistic tools available for eventual identification, however unreliable and inefficient that tool actually was in practice. By the final decades of the nineteenth century, standardized photography offered something faster, cheaper, and considerably easier to circulate between institutions, and police departments and morgues across Europe gradually adopted photographic records in place of, or alongside, the older practice of physical display and casting.

This shift had a direct and documented effect on one institution already discussed in this book: the public morgue in Paris, whose open display of unidentified bodies had, by the early twentieth century, become increasingly regarded as both impractical and, to a growing number of contemporary critics, distasteful — a form of entertainment dressed as public service. The morgue's public viewing gallery was eventually closed to casual visitors, with identification work shifting toward photographic records that could be examined, and where necessary published in newspapers, without requiring the physical, and increasingly controversial, spectacle of crowds filing past a glass partition. The underlying goal — helping the public assist in identifying the unclaimed dead — remained essentially unchanged. The method through which that goal was pursued had been transformed almost completely, moving from the physical presence of the body itself, or a plaster impression of it, toward a printed or projected image that could travel far beyond the walls of a single mortuary.

section.subtitle: When the System Failed: The Case of the Two Wests
section.paragraph: Bertillon's anthropometric system, for all its genuine methodological ambition, contained a serious and ultimately fatal flaw: it assumed that the combination of measurements it relied upon was, for practical purposes, unique to each individual, an assumption that proved considerably less reliable than its early advocates believed, particularly once the system was applied at a large scale across millions of records, and particularly in cases involving close biological relatives.

The clearest documented illustration of this weakness comes from an American case widely discussed in the history of forensic identification: in 1903, at the federal penitentiary in Leavenworth, Kansas, prison officials processing an incoming inmate named Will West found that his Bertillon measurements matched, in extraordinarily close detail, those already on file for a prisoner already incarcerated at the same institution under the very similar name William West. Investigation revealed that the two men, despite the striking similarity in both name and anthropometric measurement, were apparently unrelated individuals — though some later accounts of the case have raised the possibility of an undocumented family connection, a detail that remains genuinely uncertain in the historical record. Whatever the precise relationship between the two men, the case became, almost immediately, a powerful and widely circulated argument against the reliability of anthropometric measurement as a stand-alone identification system, since two apparently distinct individuals had produced measurements too similar to reliably distinguish between them using Bertillon's method alone.

The Leavenworth case did not, by itself, single-handedly end the use of anthropometric measurement — the practice continued in various police departments for some additional years after 1903 — but it became a frequently cited symbol of the system's fundamental limitation, arriving at almost exactly the moment when an alternative biometric technology, already under serious scientific development for over a decade, was beginning to demonstrate a level of individual uniqueness and reliability that Bertillon's careful measurements simply could not match.

section.subtitle: Fingerprints and the End of an Era
section.paragraph: That alternative technology was the fingerprint, and its rise to prominence as the dominant tool of criminal identification through the first decades of the twentieth century represents one of the genuine scientific success stories connected to this book's broader history, standing in sharp and welcome contrast to the pseudo-scientific theories of physiognomy and phrenology examined in earlier chapters. The English scientist Francis Galton, building on earlier observations by other researchers working in British India and elsewhere, published influential work in the early 1890s establishing that fingerprint patterns were both effectively permanent across an individual's lifetime and sufficiently varied to distinguish reliably between different people, and proposed a practical system for classifying and comparing prints.

Galton's classification work was subsequently refined into a more practical operational system by Edward Henry, a British police official working in colonial India, whose method — generally known as the Henry Classification System — was adopted by Scotland Yard's newly established fingerprint bureau in London in 1901, marking one of the first large-scale institutional adoptions of fingerprinting as a primary tool of criminal identification. Over the following two decades, fingerprinting spread rapidly through police forces across Europe and North America, gradually displacing Bertillon's anthropometric measurements as the preferred method of positively identifying both criminal suspects and, increasingly, unidentified bodies, a role in which fingerprints offered a significant additional advantage that neither Bertillonage nor photography could fully match: a fingerprint could, in principle, be recovered directly from a crime scene itself, independent of any prior photograph or measurement of a particular suspect, opening an entirely new category of forensic investigation that had simply not existed before.

This transition mattered directly to the story of the death mask, because it marked the effective end of any serious claim that a physical facial cast could serve a genuinely useful forensic function. Where earlier chapters in this book described death masks and skull measurements being collected in service of criminal identification, physiognomic theory, or simple morgue record-keeping, the combination of standardized photography and fingerprint classification had, by the 1910s and 1920s, rendered the death mask essentially obsolete as a practical tool of forensic science. What remained afterward — and what the rest of this book will continue to explore — was the mask's older, more enduring set of purposes: memorial, artistic, and increasingly, historical and collectible, purposes that had, in truth, motivated the practice long before criminology ever laid claim to it, and that would continue to motivate it long after criminology moved on to more reliable tools.

keypoints.title: Key Point: A Century of Identification, in Three Technologies
keypoints.point: Physical display and facial casting (early to mid-nineteenth century): slow, unreliable, dependent on chance recognition or flawed physiognomic theory.

Anthropometric measurement and standardized photography (1880s–1900s): faster and more systematic, but ultimately limited by the non-uniqueness of body measurements, as the Leavenworth case demonstrated.

Fingerprint classification (1890s onward): the first method in this sequence considered genuinely reliable by modern forensic standards, and the one that effectively ended the mask's practical role in identification.

section.subtitle: Lombroso's Skulls, and His Own
section.paragraph: No figure connects the flawed science of criminal physiognomy discussed in earlier chapters to the forensic developments of this one more directly, or more strangely, than the Italian physician and criminologist Cesare Lombroso, already introduced briefly in Chapter 1. Lombroso, working from the 1870s onward, developed an influential and now thoroughly discredited theory holding that certain individuals were, in effect, "born criminals," identifiable through specific inherited physical traits — a theory he framed as a kind of atavism, or evolutionary throwback to earlier, supposedly more primitive human types. In building his case, Lombroso assembled an extensive personal collection of skulls, photographs, and other physical evidence gathered from executed criminals and psychiatric patients, treating these individuals' remains and features as raw material for a theory that modern criminology and anthropology regard as scientifically baseless and deeply entangled with the racial and class prejudices of his era.

What makes Lombroso's story especially striking, and especially relevant to the themes of consent already raised in earlier chapters through the case of Jeremy Bentham, is that Lombroso, apparently confident in the validity of his own theories to the very end, arranged for his own remains — his skeleton and preserved brain — to be added, after his death in 1909, to the very museum collection in Turin that he had spent his career assembling, where they remain on public display today alongside the specimens he had gathered from others during his lifetime. Unlike the executed criminals and unidentified dead discussed in the previous chapter, Lombroso's own inclusion in his museum was entirely voluntary, a final act of confidence in a body of work that subsequent generations of scientists would go on to reject almost entirely. His case offers a genuinely unusual historical irony: the founder of a school of thought responsible for treating so many other people's remains as scientific specimens without their consent ultimately volunteered his own body for exactly the same treatment, apparently seeing no contradiction in the gesture at all.

section.subtitle: The Mask Loses Its Job, But Not Its Meaning
section.paragraph: It would be easy to read this chapter's story as one of straightforward technological progress displacing an older, cruder practice, and there is real truth in that reading. But it would be a mistake to conclude from this chapter that the death mask simply disappeared once photography and fingerprinting rendered it forensically obsolete. What actually happened was more interesting, and more consistent with the broader argument this book has been building since its first chapter: stripped of whatever practical identification function it had briefly, imperfectly served, the death mask was freed to be understood more clearly for what it had always primarily been, even during the decades when criminologists and phrenologists had tried to press it into scientific service — an object of memory, art, and historical commemoration, rather than a tool of evidence.

Sculptors and artists continued to take death masks of notable figures throughout the twentieth century, entirely independent of any forensic purpose. Museums continued to collect and display existing masks, increasingly for their historical, biographical, and artistic significance rather than any claim to scientific utility. And the broader public continued to find these objects emotionally compelling for exactly the reasons explored in the earliest chapters of this book: the strange, unmediated directness of a face taken from life's final moments, familiar and unsettling in equal measure. The forensic chapter of the death mask's history, in other words, turns out to have been something of a detour — an important one, worth understanding in detail, but ultimately a shorter and less central part of the mask's long story than the memorial and artistic purposes that both preceded it and outlasted it.

section.subtitle: The Morgue Behind Glass, Revisited
section.paragraph: It is worth returning briefly to the image that opened the previous chapter: the public morgue in Paris, its glass partition, its curious crowds. That institution's eventual closure to casual public viewing, discussed earlier in this chapter, marks a fitting symbolic endpoint for the specific historical period this chapter has examined. The impulse that had once sent ordinary Parisians filing past the bodies of strangers — a genuine, if often exploited, desire to help restore a name to the nameless — did not disappear when the morgue's doors closed to the public. It was redirected, gradually and imperfectly, into photographic archives, police records, and eventually the more rigorous forensic databases of the twentieth century, tools that could accomplish the same underlying goal with considerably less spectacle, and considerably more respect for the dignity of the dead than a public queue outside a mortuary window had ever really allowed.

section.subtitle: What Forensic Science Owes, and Does Not Owe, to the Death Mask
section.paragraph: It is tempting, given how closely the two subjects have been intertwined throughout this chapter, to describe modern forensic science as a direct descendant of the death mask tradition. That framing overstates the connection. Modern forensic identification, at its best, rests on principles the original death-mask and physiognomic traditions never approached: statistically grounded claims about biological uniqueness, rigorously tested and repeatedly verified, developed by scientists who, in the case of fingerprinting at least, largely succeeded in separating genuine biological evidence from the kind of unfounded character judgment that had corrupted physiognomy and phrenology from the outset. The death mask's actual contribution to this story is narrower, but still worth naming honestly: it represents the earlier, more intuitive, and considerably less rigorous ancestor of an impulse that forensic science eventually made systematic — the conviction that the physical particularities of an individual body could, in principle, distinguish that person reliably from every other person who had ever lived. The death mask tried to capture that particularity through the blunt, physical directness of plaster and wax. Fingerprint science eventually captured it through mathematics. Both, in their very different ways, pursued the same underlying question this book keeps returning to: what, physically, makes one person unmistakably themselves, and how much of that can actually survive them?

section.subtitle: What Comes Next
section.paragraph: Having followed the death mask through its forensic detour and back out the other side, this book now turns to a question that has been present since its opening pages but never yet addressed directly: how, exactly, were these objects made? The next chapter steps back from individual biographies and historical episodes to examine the material craft itself — plaster, wax, and bronze, the tools and techniques sculptors relied upon across several centuries, and the surprisingly significant ways in which the choice of material shaped not only how a death mask looked, but how faithfully, and for how long, it managed to preserve the face it had been made to remember.

chapter.title: Plaster, Wax, Bronze, and the Art of Reproducing a Face
chapter.epigraph: The material a sculptor reached for after someone died was never a neutral choice. Plaster, wax, and bronze each carried their own practical limits and their own quiet symbolism, and the object that survives today often owes as much to that choice as to the face it was meant to record.

section.subtitle: The Craft Behind the Curtain
section.paragraph: Every death mask discussed so far in this book — Napoleon's contested cast, Beethoven's familiar plaster face, the countless unidentified faces displayed at the Paris morgue — was, before it was anything else, a physical object made by a person using a particular material and a particular set of techniques. This book has, until now, kept that craft largely in the background, focusing instead on who these masks belonged to and what they came to mean. This chapter steps forward to look directly at the workshop itself: the materials sculptors relied on, the practical advantages and limitations of each, and the ways those material choices shaped which objects survived, in what condition, and how faithfully they preserved the faces they were made to remember.

This chapter will describe these materials and their general use in broad, historical terms, in keeping with the purpose of a cultural history rather than a technical manual. It does not provide, and does not intend to provide, step-by-step instructions for casting a face from human remains; the specifics of preparing or handling a body for this purpose fall well outside what this book sets out to do, and outside what any reader needs in order to understand the history and significance of the objects themselves.

section.subtitle: Plaster: The Workhorse of the Trade
section.paragraph: Of the three materials named in this chapter's title, plaster — more precisely, gypsum plaster, sometimes called plaster of Paris after the extensive gypsum deposits historically mined near the French capital — was by far the most commonly used across the centuries this book has covered. Its popularity rested on a combination of practical advantages that made it, in effect, the default medium of the trade. Gypsum plaster was relatively inexpensive and widely available, particularly in regions like the Paris basin where raw gypsum could be quarried locally and processed into fine casting powder by artisans and specialized suppliers. Mixed with water, it formed a workable paste that could be applied in a soft, moldable state and that set, hardening into a rigid, stable form, within a relatively short window of time — a crucial practical advantage for a craft that so often had to work quickly, in the limited hours before a recently deceased face began to change.

Once set and carefully removed, a plaster negative mold could itself be used to produce one or more positive casts, typically also in plaster, though the material of the final positive cast could vary depending on the sculptor's intentions. Plaster's relative cheapness and speed made it the natural choice for the vast majority of death masks discussed throughout this book, from Beethoven's mask in 1827 Vienna to the countless less famous casts taken in police mortuaries and private homes across nineteenth-century Europe. Its principal drawback lay not in the casting process itself but in its long-term durability: plaster is a comparatively brittle, porous material, vulnerable to chipping, cracking, moisture damage, and surface discoloration over years and decades of handling, storage, and display, a vulnerability that has created real and ongoing challenges for the museums and conservators who care for these objects today, a subject this chapter will return to later on.

keypoints.title: Key Point: Comparing the Three Materials
keypoints.point: Plaster: cheap, quick to work with, widely available — but comparatively fragile and prone to long-term damage, making it the most common but often the least well preserved of the three materials over time.

Wax: capable of an unusually lifelike, translucent surface quality that closely resembled skin — but soft, temperature-sensitive, and vulnerable to melting, warping, or insect damage, limiting how many original wax masks survive intact today.

Bronze: durable and essentially permanent once cast — but a more expensive, technically demanding secondary process, generally used to reproduce an existing plaster or wax mold rather than to take a direct impression from a face.

section.subtitle: What the Cast Could Not Show
section.paragraph: It is worth pausing here to acknowledge, without dwelling on it in graphic detail, that the casting process placed real and sometimes considerable strain on everyone involved. Family members present in the room, already grieving, had to tolerate the practical business of a stranger's hands working over the face of someone they loved. Sculptors themselves, working against time and often under emotional pressure from the family, could not always achieve the technically ideal result; historical accounts and surviving objects both suggest that hair was occasionally caught and damaged in the setting plaster, that skin could be marked or bruised during the careful process of separating a set mold from a face, and that some casting attempts were simply unsuccessful, requiring a second attempt or producing a final result the family considered unsatisfactory and chose not to preserve or display. None of this diminishes the historical value of the objects that did survive successfully. It is a reminder, consistent with points raised in earlier chapters, that a death mask was never a simple, effortless, mechanically perfect transcription of a face — it was the product of a difficult, sometimes imperfect human process, undertaken under some of the most emotionally charged circumstances imaginable.

section.subtitle: Wax and the Illusion of Living Skin
section.paragraph: Wax offered sculptors something plaster could not: a surface quality with genuine translucency, capable of suggesting the subtle glow of living skin in a way that opaque, chalky plaster never quite managed. This quality made wax an especially prized material for portrait busts and effigies intended for close, ongoing display, including the royal funeral effigies discussed in an earlier chapter, and it connected the death-mask tradition to a broader and genuinely fascinating culture of wax modeling that flourished in parts of Europe, particularly Italy, from the eighteenth century onward. In Florence, the anatomical wax models produced under sculptors such as Clemente Susini for the museum today known as La Specola achieved a level of anatomical detail and lifelike color so precise that they were used for genuine medical instruction, allowing students to study the structures of the human body in a level of vivid, three-dimensional detail that no illustration could fully match, without requiring the constant availability of actual cadavers. A related tradition, sometimes called moulage, produced detailed wax models of diseased tissue and skin conditions for use in medical teaching collections well into the twentieth century — a practice adjacent to, though distinct from, the death mask tradition proper, sharing its underlying material and, in a sense, its underlying instinct: that a carefully colored, textured wax surface could preserve visual medical information more vividly and durably than any two-dimensional image.

Wax's expressive advantages came at a real practical cost. It is a soft, temperature-sensitive material, vulnerable to warping or even melting under heat, prone to gradual discoloration and cracking with age, and, unlike plaster, attractive to certain insects and pests capable of damaging its surface over long storage. As a result, far fewer original wax death masks have survived in good condition across the centuries compared to their plaster counterparts, and many wax funeral effigies and masks known to historians through written and visual records no longer exist in their original form at all, having deteriorated, been damaged, or been deliberately replaced over the generations — a pattern of loss this chapter will return to shortly, when it turns to how museums and conservators think about "original" and "copy" today.

section.subtitle: From Plaster to Permanence: The Turn to Bronze
section.paragraph: Bronze occupies a different position in this material history altogether. Unlike plaster and wax, bronze was almost never used to take a direct impression from a face; the metal-casting process required for bronze work involves intense heat entirely unsuited to contact with human skin, living or dead. Instead, bronze entered this story as a secondary material, used to produce especially durable, permanent reproductions from an existing plaster or wax original, through a casting process — closely related to methods used in bronze sculpture generally, including the long-established lost-wax casting technique — that could faithfully translate the fine surface detail of an original mold into a metal object capable of lasting, essentially unchanged, for centuries.

This durability made bronze the material of choice whenever a death mask was intended for permanent public display, incorporation into a monument or memorial, or long-term preservation in a major museum or institutional collection, and it explains why some of the most widely reproduced and publicly familiar death-mask images in this book's story — including versions of masks associated with figures such as Napoleon and Beethoven — exist today in bronze editions produced sometime after the original plaster casting, sometimes considerably later, based on the original mold or an early plaster cast taken from it. This creates a genuinely important point of historical nuance that this book has returned to repeatedly and will return to again: in a meaningful number of cases, the object a visitor encounters today in a museum case, admired as though it were the direct, unmediated product of a single historical moment, is in fact a later bronze reproduction, one or more removes from the original plaster impression taken from the actual face — durable, faithful in surface detail, and historically significant in its own right, but not, in the strictest sense, the same physical object that first touched the deceased.

keypoints.title: Key Point: The Copy That Outlives the Original
keypoints.point: Bronze's durability means that bronze reproductions of famous death masks have, in a number of documented cases, survived in better condition than the original plaster or wax mold used to create them.

This means the object most visible to the public today — often prominently displayed, confidently labeled — may be a later, if faithful, reproduction rather than the first physical impression taken from the deceased.
Recognizing this does not diminish these bronze casts' historical and artistic value; it simply requires being precise about what, exactly, a given object represents.

section.subtitle: The Traveling Trade in Plaster Faces
section.paragraph: Alongside the individually commissioned masks of specific historical figures examined throughout this book, plaster's affordability supported an entire, less prestigious commercial trade that deserves mention here. From at least the early nineteenth century onward, itinerant sellers — many of them Italian craftsmen working a well-documented trade sometimes referred to by the Italian term *figurinai* — traveled across European towns and cities selling small, mass-produced plaster busts, statuettes, and, in some cases, reproductions of well-known death masks, to a general public eager for affordable versions of images otherwise associated with wealth, fame, or scholarly institutions. A middle-class household in nineteenth-century England or France might display a modestly priced plaster reproduction of Napoleon's or a favorite poet's death mask on a parlor shelf, purchased not from a sculptor's private commission but from a traveling cart or a shop specializing in this kind of affordable decorative reproduction. This commercial trade illustrates something this book has emphasized before: that by the height of the nineteenth-century death-mask culture, these objects had moved well beyond their origins as private memorial commissions, becoming, for a significant portion of the European public, an ordinary and widely available category of domestic decoration and popular commemoration, produced and sold at a considerable remove from the original, more intimate act of casting.

section.subtitle: Materials as Meaning
section.paragraph: Beyond their practical properties, the three materials examined in this chapter carried distinct symbolic associations that shaped how contemporaries understood the objects made from them, even if this symbolism was rarely stated explicitly at the time. Plaster, cheap and workaday, carried an implicit democratic or at least practical character — the material of the ordinary, functional death mask, accessible to families and institutions without great wealth, and correspondingly, the material in which the vast majority of masks discussed throughout this book, famous and anonymous alike, were actually produced. Wax, with its lifelike translucency and its genuine physical impermanence — its literal vulnerability to melting and decay — carried an almost poetic appropriateness to its subject matter that contemporary observers occasionally noted directly: a material that could itself dissolve and disappear, used to memorialize a person who had already done exactly that. Bronze, by contrast, carried associations of permanence, civic honor, and public commemoration inherited directly from its long prior history in monumental sculpture and portrait busts of the powerful; a death mask reproduced in bronze implicitly asserted that its subject deserved to be remembered not just privately, within a family or a scholarly collection, but publicly and more or less permanently, in the same material tradition as the statues of generals and monarchs that had lined European public squares for centuries before.

section.subtitle: Conserving a Face Twice Removed
section.paragraph: The material realities explored throughout this chapter carry direct consequences for the museums, conservators, and archivists who care for these objects today, work already touched on in earlier chapters and examined in far greater depth in a later chapter of this book devoted specifically to museum collections and their ethics. A plaster mask that has survived for a century and a half has typically survived several rounds of handling, minor damage, and repair, sometimes performed by skilled conservators using techniques and materials well documented in institutional records, and sometimes performed decades or centuries earlier by less careful hands, using methods that are difficult to fully reconstruct today. Conservators examining a historic death mask must often work to distinguish original nineteenth-century plaster from later restoration filler, original surface texture from a later, well-meaning but historically inaccurate touch-up, and, in the case of masks that survive in multiple plaster, wax, and bronze versions across different collections, must grapple directly with the question raised earlier in this chapter: which surviving object, if any, most closely represents the original moment of casting, and how much does that distinction actually matter to the object's historical and cultural significance today.

This is not merely a technical or academic puzzle. It bears directly on how confidently a museum can label an object, how a historian can respectfully and accurately describe it to the public, and how honestly this book itself has tried, throughout its preceding chapters, to distinguish documented fact from confident-sounding tradition whenever the two diverge. The material history explored in this chapter is, in the end, inseparable from the questions of authenticity and evidence that have run through this book from its opening pages.

section.subtitle: What Comes Next
section.paragraph: Having examined the materials and methods behind these objects, this book now turns to some of the specific masks whose stories have become genuinely mysterious — cases where disputed attribution, lost documentation, or outright historical uncertainty have left researchers and museums without confident answers about a mask's true origin, its authenticity, or even, in some instances, the identity of the face it claims to represent. The next chapter gathers several of these cases together, examining what can be verified, what remains genuinely unresolved, and what these unresolved mysteries reveal about the limits of even the most careful historical scholarship applied to an object as intimate, and as easily misattributed, as a human face preserved in plaster, wax, or bronze.

chapter.title: Famous Masks, Lost Identities, and Historical Mysteries
chapter.epigraph: Not every death mask in a museum case is what its label claims. Some are honest reproductions of honest originals. Others are the product of wishful thinking, commercial ambition, or simple confusion, repeated so often across the generations that the confusion itself became a kind of tradition.

section.subtitle: A Museum of Doubt
section.paragraph: If the preceding chapters have established anything clearly, it is that the history of the death mask cannot be told as a simple sequence of verified facts. Nearly every chapter so far has paused, at some point, to separate documented evidence from popular tradition, disputed attribution, or outright legend — the uncertain provenance of Napoleon's several surviving casts, the doubtful reliability of Madame Tussaud's own later account of her work during the French Revolution, the unresolved question of who exactly the Unknown Woman of the Seine actually was. This chapter gathers several additional cases where that gap between reputation and evidence becomes not just a passing complication, but the entire story worth telling. These are masks, heads, and preserved remains whose fame rests, in large part, precisely on the mystery surrounding them.

section.subtitle: The Face That May Not Be Shakespeare's
section.paragraph: Among the most persistently discussed disputed objects in this entire history is the so-called Kesselstadt Death Mask, a plaster cast that surfaced in Germany in 1849, when it was discovered among the belongings of a noble family, the Kesselstadts, bearing a painted inscription including the date 1616 — the same year William Shakespeare died in Stratford-upon-Avon. The mask's resemblance to established portraits of Shakespeare, combined with the matching date, generated enormous excitement among scholars and the public alike when it was first publicized, and the object has continued to attract serious, if largely inconclusive, scholarly attention ever since.

The case for authenticity has never been especially strong, judged by the standards this book has tried to apply consistently throughout. There is no contemporary seventeenth-century documentation describing a death mask being taken from Shakespeare's face at all, a striking absence given how much scholarly effort has gone into reconstructing the details of Shakespeare's life and death from surviving records. The inscribed date on the mask itself has been subjected to close physical and stylistic examination, with some specialists arguing the lettering style is inconsistent with genuine early seventeenth-century practice, suggesting a later addition intended to enhance the object's apparent significance, whether through innocent misattribution or more deliberate embellishment. Facial comparison with the small number of portraits reasonably accepted as authentic depictions of Shakespeare — themselves a subject of ongoing scholarly debate — has produced genuine disagreement rather than consensus, with some researchers finding meaningful resemblance and others finding the comparison unconvincing.

Most Shakespeare scholars today treat the Kesselstadt mask with considerable skepticism, regarding it as, at best, an unproven and probably unprovable claim, and at worst, a later fabrication or honest misattribution that gained momentum simply because the idea of a surviving physical trace of Shakespeare's actual face proved too appealing to resist. The mask continues to be exhibited and discussed, and reproductions of it remain widely available, but it stands today as a useful illustration of a pattern this book has now traced through several chapters: an object's persistent popularity and its actual evidentiary strength are, disappointingly often, almost entirely unrelated to one another.

keypoints.title: Key Point: What a Genuine Attribution Actually Requires
keypoints.point: Contemporary documentation describing the casting itself, ideally naming who made it, when, and under what circumstances.
A continuous, traceable chain of ownership connecting the object from its claimed origin to its present location, without unexplained gaps.
Physical and stylistic analysis consistent with the claimed period of creation, rather than later materials, techniques, or lettering styles.
The Kesselstadt mask fails, or at minimum cannot satisfy, most of these tests, which is precisely why serious scholars remain unconvinced despite the object's enduring popular appeal.

section.subtitle: The Mask That Was Never Made: Mozart's Missing Face
section.paragraph: A different, and in some ways more instructive, kind of mystery surrounds the composer Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, who died in Vienna in December 1791. Popular imagination has long assumed, understandably given how thoroughly this book has documented the death-mask tradition surrounding other major composers, that a death mask of Mozart must exist somewhere, waiting to be properly recognized. The historical record does not support this assumption. Mozart was buried, in keeping with common Viennese burial customs of the period for individuals of his social and financial standing, in a common grave rather than an individually marked plot, and no reliable contemporary source describes a death mask being taken from his face at the time of his death. Various objects have, over the subsequent two centuries, been proposed or rumored as possible Mozart death masks or life masks, but none has achieved anything close to scholarly consensus regarding authenticity, and the most careful modern assessments generally conclude that no credible death mask of Mozart survives, if one was ever made at all.

This case is worth including specifically because it inverts the pattern of the Kesselstadt mask. Rather than a specific, disputed physical object commanding ongoing debate, Mozart's case involves the near-total absence of any object at all, standing in tension with a persistent popular belief that one ought to exist. The gap between what people assume must be true, given a figure's fame and the era's documented customs, and what the historical record actually supports is, in its own way, just as revealing as the more dramatic controversies surrounding objects like the Kesselstadt mask. It is a reminder that even genuinely well-documented historical periods and figures can leave real, permanent gaps in the physical record, gaps that popular memory tends to fill with confident assumption rather than comfortable uncertainty.

section.subtitle: A Head With No Mask At All: Cromwell's Long Journey
section.paragraph: Some of the strangest stories in this book's broader territory involve not a cast taken from a face, but the astonishing post-mortem fate of an actual preserved head — a case that belongs in this chapter precisely because it illustrates, in unusually vivid and well-documented form, the same questions of authenticity, provenance, and custody that surround the disputed masks already discussed. Oliver Cromwell, the military and political leader who governed England as Lord Protector following the execution of King Charles I, died of natural causes in 1658 and was given an elaborate state funeral and burial at Westminster Abbey. Following the restoration of the monarchy under Charles II in 1660, however, Cromwell's body was exhumed in an act of deliberate political retribution, subjected to a posthumous ritual of execution, and his head was severed and displayed on a pole outside Westminster Hall, where, according to well-documented historical accounts, it remained on public view for a number of years.

What followed is a genuinely remarkable, if grim, chain of custody, traceable through a sequence of private owners, collectors, and exhibitors across the following three centuries: the head reportedly blew down from its pole at some point and was recovered by a soldier, subsequently passing through a series of private hands, occasional public exhibition as a curiosity, and periods of more discreet, private ownership, before eventually being acquired by descendants of the Cromwell family in the early twentieth century. Scientific examination conducted in the 1930s, comparing the preserved head against Cromwell's known portraits and the documented historical account of his death and burial, concluded that the head was very likely genuine, and it was finally given a formal, permanent burial in 1960 in the grounds of Sidney Sussex College, Cambridge, Cromwell's own college as a young man, at a location that has been kept deliberately unmarked and undisclosed in order to prevent any further disturbance.

Cromwell's case does not involve a death mask in the technical sense this book has used throughout, but it belongs squarely within this chapter's larger concerns. It demonstrates, in an unusually extreme and well-documented form, how thoroughly a society's treatment of a notable person's physical remains can be driven by political meaning rather than simple commemoration, how many hands and how much uncertainty can accumulate around even a genuinely authenticated relic across several centuries, and how modern scientific examination — comparable in spirit to the authenticity assessments applied to disputed masks like the Kesselstadt cast — can eventually bring a measure of confident resolution to a story that spent centuries as pure rumor and curiosity.

section.subtitle: The Business of Believing: How Fake Masks Enter the Market
section.paragraph: The Shakespeare and Mozart cases, taken together, point toward a broader pattern worth naming directly: throughout the period this book examines, and particularly during the height of nineteenth-century collecting culture already discussed in earlier chapters, there existed real commercial incentive to produce, or simply to claim, death masks of famous historical figures, regardless of whether reliable evidence actually supported the attribution. A plaster cast confidently labeled as the death mask of a beloved poet, composer, or historical hero commanded far greater interest, and far greater commercial value, than an honestly labeled later reconstruction or an object of genuinely uncertain origin. This incentive did not necessarily require outright, deliberate fraud in every case; honest confusion, optimistic wishful thinking passed down across generations of ownership, and the simple, gradual erosion of accurate provenance records over decades of private sale and inheritance could all produce the same practical result as intentional forgery, an object confidently presented to the public as something the available evidence does not actually support.

This pattern has left modern museums, auction houses, and historians with an ongoing, genuinely difficult task: assessing claimed death masks not by their popular reputation or the confidence of their existing labels, but through the kind of careful, multi-pronged verification process outlined earlier in this chapter's discussion of the Kesselstadt mask — documentary evidence, unbroken provenance, and physical and stylistic analysis consistent with the claimed period of origin. Where that verification succeeds, as with the Cromwell head's twentieth-century scientific examination, a long-uncertain object can be given a genuinely confident historical identity. Where it fails, or where the evidence remains permanently too thin to resolve one way or the other, honest historical practice requires living with the uncertainty rather than resolving it through confident assertion, however unsatisfying that uncertainty might be to museum visitors hoping for a definitive answer.

section.subtitle: Relics Beyond the Face: Hearts, Fingers, and the Wider Cult of Remains
section.paragraph: It is worth briefly widening the lens here, because the impulse driving the death mask tradition examined throughout this book did not confine itself to faces alone, and understanding that broader context helps explain why claims like the Kesselstadt mask found such a receptive public in the first place. The desire to retain some direct physical connection to a revered figure after death produced, across the same historical period, a wider and genuinely striking culture of preserving other bodily fragments of the notable dead. Frédéric Chopin's heart, removed following his death in 1849 according to his own reported wishes and the customs of the period, was transported to Warsaw and sealed within a pillar of the Holy Cross Church, where it remains today, periodically the subject of renewed scholarly and medical interest regarding the cause of his final illness. The astronomer and physicist Galileo Galilei, who died in 1642, had several fingers, a tooth, and a section of vertebra removed from his remains during a documented eighteenth-century exhumation and reburial, relics that were subsequently displayed and, after passing through private hands for over a century, eventually reunited and placed on public display at the Museo Galileo in Florence.

These relics operated according to a logic closely related to, though distinct from, the death mask tradition examined throughout this book: where a death mask preserved the appearance of a face, these physical relics preserved a literal, unmediated fragment of the person themselves, offering an even more direct, if considerably more unsettling to modern sensibilities, form of physical connection to a revered historical figure. Understanding this wider culture of relic preservation helps explain why claims surrounding objects like the Kesselstadt mask found such fertile ground among nineteenth-century audiences already primed, by a well-established broader tradition, to believe that a direct physical trace of a beloved historical figure might plausibly have survived, waiting to be rediscovered.

section.subtitle: What These Mysteries Have in Common
section.paragraph: Considered together, the cases gathered in this chapter — a disputed mask, a mask that most likely never existed at all, an authenticated head with an extraordinary and well-documented chain of custody, and a wider culture of bodily relics extending well beyond the face — share a single underlying dynamic that this book has returned to from its opening pages. The desire to hold onto some direct, physical trace of a person who mattered is powerful enough to generate not only genuine, carefully documented historical objects, but also honest confusion, wishful misattribution, and outright commercial fabrication, often in roughly equal measure, and frequently tangled together within the history of a single object. Separating one from the other requires exactly the kind of patient, unglamorous documentary and physical analysis this book has tried to model throughout its preceding chapters: checking dates against known biography, tracing ownership across generations, comparing surviving portraits with careful attention rather than eager assumption, and, perhaps most importantly, remaining genuinely willing to conclude, as the honest answer regarding Shakespeare's disputed mask and Mozart's missing one both ultimately require, that the true and complete answer may simply be that we do not, and quite possibly cannot, know for certain.

That uncertainty is not a failure of this book, or of the historians and conservators whose careful work it draws upon. It is, in its own way, as central to the real history of the death mask as any confidently attributed, well-documented object examined in the chapters before this one — a reminder that even our deepest, most persistent desire to hold onto the face of someone we have lost does not, by itself, guarantee that what survives is genuinely theirs.

chapter.title: Museums, Collections, Ethics, and the Afterlife of the Dead
chapter.epigraph: A death mask does not stop accumulating history the moment it is cast. It keeps being owned, displayed, argued over, and reassessed, sometimes for centuries longer than the person it depicts was ever alive.

section.subtitle: From Studio Shelf to Glass Case
section.paragraph: Nearly every mask examined in this book has followed some version of the same broad trajectory: made in private, in the immediate aftermath of a death, by a sculptor working for a grieving family, a scientific institution, or the state, and only later — sometimes within years, sometimes only after a century or more of private ownership — finding its way into the kind of public museum or university collection where most readers of this book have likely encountered a death mask for themselves. That final step, from private object to public artifact, is not a neutral or automatic one. It involves decisions, made by specific people and institutions, about what an object means, who has the right to hold and display it, and what obligations, if any, the institution takes on toward both the historical record and the memory of the person the object represents.

This chapter turns directly to those decisions, and to the broader, still unresolved questions of ethics and stewardship that now surround death masks and related human remains held in museum and university collections around the world. It draws together threads raised throughout the preceding chapters — the consent so rarely granted by the condemned and the unidentified, the scientific ambitions that once justified collecting the skulls and faces of criminals, the commercial trade that turned private grief into a marketable curiosity — and asks what responsible modern institutions owe to all of it now.

section.subtitle: A Question the Object Cannot Answer for Itself
section.paragraph: The question of consent, raised at several points earlier in this book, deserves to be gathered together explicitly here, because it sits at the center of nearly every serious ethical debate modern museums now have about these collections. The range of circumstances under which the masks discussed in this book were made is genuinely wide. Jeremy Bentham, examined in an earlier chapter, explicitly and deliberately consented in advance to the display of his own preserved remains, leaving detailed instructions in his will. Beethoven's and Chopin's families, by contrast, commissioned masks of their loved ones without any documented instruction from the deceased themselves on the matter, acting instead from grief and a desire for commemoration that most modern readers would likely find sympathetic and understandable, even without formal consent from the person being cast. The executed criminals whose skulls and faces filled nineteenth-century phrenological collections had no meaningful opportunity to consent or object at all, their bodies treated as a further extension of a punishment the state had already decided they deserved. And the unidentified dead displayed at institutions like the Paris morgue existed in a kind of consent vacuum entirely: no family present to grant or withhold permission, no documented wishes of any kind, simply an anonymous body processed according to institutional necessity.

A responsible modern institution holding objects from across this entire spectrum cannot apply a single, uniform ethical standard to all of them, because the objects themselves did not originate under a single, uniform set of circumstances. This has pushed many museums and universities toward a more case-by-case, deliberately researched approach to their collections — examining, wherever possible, exactly how and under what circumstances a given mask or set of remains was originally obtained, and using that research to inform decisions about display, description, and, in some cases, whether the institution should continue to hold the object at all.

keypoints.title: Key Point: Not All Masks Carry the Same Ethical Weight
keypoints.point: Voluntary, explicit consent (Bentham's auto-icon): the clearest ethical case, though even here questions remain about how future generations should honor a centuries-old personal wish.

Family-commissioned memorial masks (Beethoven, Chopin, and most of the masks examined in this book): made without the direct consent of the deceased, but within a recognizable and broadly sympathetic tradition of grief and commemoration.
State-collected masks of the condemned: made under conditions of essentially total power imbalance, with the subject unable to object in any meaningful sense.
Masks of the unidentified: made in the complete absence of any consenting party at all, raising distinct questions about who, if anyone, can meaningfully speak for the deceased today.

section.subtitle: The Museum That Had to Reckon With Itself
section.paragraph: Few institutions illustrate the practical stakes of this ethical reassessment more directly than the Museum of Criminal Anthropology in Turin, the very collection assembled by Cesare Lombroso and examined in an earlier chapter, which today holds not only the skulls, casts, and photographs Lombroso gathered from executed criminals and psychiatric patients over the course of his career, but Lombroso's own donated skeleton and preserved brain as well. The museum's modern curators face an unusually direct version of a challenge shared by many institutions holding similar nineteenth-century scientific collections: how to preserve and present historically significant material — material that documents, in vivid and irreplaceable physical form, exactly how a deeply flawed and often prejudiced scientific movement actually operated — without either endorsing the discredited theories the collection was originally built to support, or simply hiding the collection away as too uncomfortable to display at all.

The approach adopted by institutions in this position, including the Turin museum, has generally involved substantial contextual reframing rather than either uncritical display or outright removal: extensive interpretive material explaining the racist and pseudo-scientific assumptions that shaped the original collection, explicit acknowledgment that the individuals represented in the collection could not consent to their inclusion, and a deliberate curatorial shift toward presenting the museum itself as a historical artifact of a discredited scientific movement, rather than as a straightforward scientific resource in the tradition Lombroso himself had intended. This reframing does not resolve every ethical tension the collection raises — critics have continued to debate whether display of these remains under any interpretive framing adequately respects the individuals involved, particularly given how thoroughly their inclusion in the collection violated the standards of consent modern institutions claim to uphold — but it represents a genuine, ongoing attempt to hold two things true at once: that the collection retains real historical and educational value, and that the circumstances of its creation were genuinely unjust.

section.subtitle: Law Catches Up: Regulating Human Remains in Collections
section.paragraph: Museum practice in this area has increasingly been shaped by formal legal frameworks, rather than institutional discretion alone. In the United Kingdom, for example, the Human Tissue Act, passed in 2004 following a series of earlier controversies over the retention of human tissue and organs without adequate consent, established a formal legal framework governing the storage, display, and use of human remains less than one hundred years old, including specific licensing requirements for public display, and created formal guidance encouraging, though not always strictly requiring, similar standards of care and documentation for older remains as well. Comparable legal and regulatory frameworks, varying considerably in their specific requirements, have developed in other countries, generally reflecting a broader international shift, accelerating from the late twentieth century onward, toward treating human remains held in museum and scientific collections as subject to genuine ethical and legal obligation, rather than simply as scientific or artistic property belonging outright to the institution that happened to possess them.

This legal evolution has directly affected how institutions approach the kinds of objects examined throughout this book. A death mask itself, being a plaster, wax, or bronze reproduction rather than actual human tissue, typically falls outside the strictest provisions of laws like the UK's Human Tissue Act, which is generally concerned with genuine bodily material. But masks are frequently held and displayed alongside genuine human remains — skulls, preserved organs, and in cases like Lombroso's own donated brain, actual anatomical material — within the same collections and often the same physical displays, meaning that institutions holding significant death-mask collections have generally had to develop broader ethical and legal policies covering their collections as a whole, rather than treating masks as entirely exempt from the more serious obligations attached to actual human remains.

section.subtitle: To Display or Not to Display
section.paragraph: For institutions holding these collections today, the practical question of what to actually put on public view, and how, has become a genuinely difficult and actively debated area of museum practice. Several distinct approaches have emerged across different institutions, each carrying its own advantages and its own critics. Some museums have chosen to continue displaying disputed or ethically fraught material largely as before, adding contextual signage and interpretive material — the approach broadly taken by the Lombroso museum — on the reasoning that removing the objects from view risks erasing an important and uncomfortable history rather than confronting it honestly. Others have moved more sensitive material out of permanent public galleries and into restricted access collections, available to researchers and scholars under specific application but no longer part of the general visitor experience, a compromise intended to preserve the material's research value while limiting its exposure as public spectacle. A smaller number of institutions have gone further still, choosing in specific, carefully considered cases to return particular remains to descendant communities or, where no such community can be meaningfully identified, to arrange respectful burial or other disposition, effectively ending the object's institutional life altogether.

None of these approaches has emerged as a clear, universally accepted standard, and this book does not attempt to argue that one is straightforwardly correct. The right answer, in the judgment of most museum ethicists working in this area today, appears to depend heavily on the specific circumstances of each object: how it was obtained, whether identifiable descendants or communities exist and what their own wishes are, how significant the object's historical or scientific value genuinely is, and how effectively an institution can actually provide the kind of careful contextual framing that makes continued display defensible rather than merely convenient.

keypoints.title: Key Point: Three Common Institutional Approaches
keypoints.point: Continued display with expanded context: preserves public access and confronts difficult history directly, but risks normalizing continued exhibition of objects obtained without consent.

Restricted research access: limits the object's exposure as public spectacle while preserving its scholarly value, though it removes the material from the kind of public engagement that can also serve genuine educational purposes.

Repatriation or respectful disposition: directly addresses the original absence of consent, but is only meaningful where identifiable descendants or communities exist to receive the remains, and permanently forecloses future historical and scientific study.

section.subtitle: Provenance Now: What Museums Owe the Objects They Hold
section.paragraph: The disputed masks examined in the previous chapter — the Kesselstadt cast claimed as Shakespeare's, the various competing versions of Napoleon's death mask — point toward a second, related obligation that has become increasingly central to responsible museum practice: rigorous, honestly documented provenance research, conducted and published with the same transparency this book has tried to model throughout its own account of these objects. Where earlier generations of museum curators were often content to display an object under whatever attribution had accompanied it into the collection, contemporary museum practice increasingly expects institutions to actively research, and honestly publish, exactly what can and cannot be verified about an object's origin, including cases where that research undermines a treasured, long-standing attribution the museum itself had previously promoted.

This shift reflects a broader professional recognition, well established in museum ethics literature by the early twenty-first century, that an institution's credibility depends on this kind of honesty, even when it is commercially or reputationally inconvenient. A museum that continues to display a disputed mask under a confident, unqualified attribution it privately knows to be unsupported by the evidence is not simply making an interpretive choice; it is participating in exactly the kind of confident-sounding misinformation this book has tried to identify and correct throughout its account of figures like Shakespeare, Dante, and the many contested versions of Napoleon's cast.

section.subtitle: The Private Market and Its Different Rules
section.paragraph: It is worth noting directly that the ethical and legal frameworks discussed in this chapter apply far more consistently, and far more strictly, to public museums and universities than to the private market in historical death masks, which continues to operate today through auction houses, specialist dealers, and private collectors, generally subject to considerably less regulatory oversight and considerably less consistent standards of provenance research than major public institutions maintain. Historic death masks, along with related material such as life masks and cast reproductions of famous faces, continue to appear at auction and in private sale on a fairly regular basis, valued by collectors for reasons ranging from genuine historical interest to the same kind of morbid, intimate fascination this book has traced back to the earliest chapters of its story.

This private market operates under a different and generally weaker set of incentives than public institutions face. A private collector or dealer has far less obligation, whether legal or reputational, to conduct or publish rigorous provenance research before offering an object for sale, and the same commercial pressures that historically encouraged confident, insufficiently supported attributions — discussed at length in the previous chapter's account of the market for supposed masks of famous historical figures — continue to operate in the contemporary private market largely unchanged. Buyers in this market, whether private collectors or, on occasion, museums acquiring new material, generally bear the primary responsibility for conducting their own due diligence regarding an object's authenticity and history, a considerably less reliable safeguard than the more formalized research standards increasingly expected of major public institutions.

section.subtitle: Scanning Instead of Touching: Digital Preservation
section.paragraph: One genuinely promising development in recent decades offers a partial resolution to some of the tensions this chapter has examined, without fully resolving the underlying ethical questions. High-resolution three-dimensional scanning technology now allows museums and researchers to create extremely detailed digital models of fragile physical masks, capturing surface detail with a level of precision that can support serious scholarly study, public digital access, and even physical reproduction through modern printing techniques, all without requiring the kind of repeated physical handling that has historically damaged fragile plaster and wax originals over generations of use. Several major collections holding significant death-mask material have begun digitizing their most historically important and physically vulnerable objects, making detailed digital models available to researchers and the public alike, while the fragile physical originals themselves are handled far less frequently and preserved instead in carefully controlled storage conditions.

Digitization does not resolve the deeper ethical questions this chapter has examined regarding consent, display, and repatriation — a perfect digital scan of a mask taken from an executed criminal without any consent raises many of the same underlying questions as the physical object itself, simply in a new and more widely distributable form, and some ethicists have specifically raised concerns about whether unrestricted digital reproduction of sensitive human-remains-adjacent material might actually increase inappropriate circulation and use rather than limiting it. But as a tool for reducing physical damage to irreplaceable historical objects, and for expanding legitimate scholarly and educational access without requiring an object to leave secure, carefully monitored storage, digital preservation represents a genuinely valuable addition to the conservation practices this book examined in an earlier chapter, one that would have been entirely unavailable to the museums and collectors who first assembled these collections across the eighteenth, nineteenth, and early twentieth centuries.

section.subtitle: What We Choose to Keep, and Why
section.paragraph: The questions raised throughout this chapter do not resolve into a tidy conclusion, and that absence of resolution is itself an accurate reflection of where serious museum ethics on this subject currently stands. Institutions holding death masks and related human remains today are, in most well-run cases, no longer operating under the confident, largely unexamined assumptions that guided the original nineteenth-century collectors this book has spent so many chapters describing — the phrenologists convinced they were advancing legitimate science, the morgue administrators convinced public display served an unambiguous public good, the private collectors and dealers largely indifferent to the question of consent altogether. In their place has come a far more careful, far more self-critical, and still genuinely unsettled set of institutional practices, shaped by law, by professional ethics, by ongoing scholarly debate, and by the ongoing, case-by-case work of curators and conservators trying to honor both the historical significance of what they hold and the basic dignity of the people those objects were once, however briefly and however imperfectly, a direct physical trace of.

chapter.title: The Enduring Fascination with the Death Mask
